title: [Vantage Point] Can BPI earn back its premium?
summary: For shareholders, true confidence will come from dependable, cash-backed profits after all credit costs are absorbed, not from the fleeting euphoria of a one-day market rally

blocks.text: (In case you missed, read the first part of this series here.)
The loan book that Maria Cristina “Ginbee” Go is preparing to inherit will ultimately determine what Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) shareholders truly own.
Investors now face the critical task of pricing a franchise whose aggressive balance sheet expansion is still revealing its full credit costs.

A sharp rally on November 4 lifted BPI shares by 7.93% to P100 on 3.04 million shares traded. While the stock remains 13.87% below its end-2025 level, excluding dividends, it now sits 6.38% above the P94 mark recorded when this analysis was first drafted.

Yet a climbing quotation makes the valuation question considerably more demanding, not less. The one-day surge visibly outpaced the Philippine Stock Exchange index’s 1.26% gain, as well as peer advances of 4.39% in Metrobank and 2.27% in BDO.
These comparisons establish clear outperformance on the trading board, but they tell us little about its fundamental catalyst.
Without concrete evidence linking the buying wave to executive moves, fresh credit disclosures, or a definitive corporate transaction, investors should resist adopting convenient narratives.
A rising share price can anticipate operational improvement, but it cannot substitute for verifiable cash collections, durable earnings, and transparent capital disclosures.

At P100, BPI’s 5.296 billion outstanding shares command a market capitalization of approximately P529.64 billion. That valuation translates to 1.10 times the bank’s June book value of P91.11 per share, compared to 1.29 times book value at the close of 2025.

September’s P488.6 billion headline equity still requires detailed reconciliation against common-shareholder equity, and June book value represents neither tangible book value — after deducting goodwill and other intangibles — nor a current liquidation estimate.
Annualizing nine-month headline net profit of P48.9 billion yields P65.2 billion, pointing to an apparent screening price-to-earnings multiple of 8.12 times.
Yet this metric is neither a trailing nor a forward forecast P/E.

Fourth-quarter credit provisions, seasonal adjustments, and earnings attributable specifically to common shareholders must all be rigorously reconciled before an apparently modest multiple can be declared a defensible bargain.
To be sure, the underlying franchise continues to expand. Gross revenue grew 9.8% over the first nine months, supported by a 13.6% expansion in loan portfolios and a 15.5% increase in fee income.
But credit provisions surged 69.2% to P19.88 billion, operating expenses outpaced top-line revenue, and net profit slipped 3.1%.
The bank is generating substantially more business, but that volume has not translated into higher bottom-line earnings.

There are qualified signs of relief. Quarterly provisions eased to P6.54 billion from P7.84 billion, helping third-quarter net income reach P16.07 billion. Pre-provision operating profit, however, slipped from P27.96 billion to P27.23 billion. Lower credit charges provided bottom-line support without demonstrating that troubled lending vintages had definitively rounded the corner.
September’s non-performing loan ratio for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) climbed to 15.62%, though the SME segment accounts for only 2.7% of the total loan portfolio.
Credit cards edged up to 5.44%, while personal lending and microfinance showed relative improvement at 6.99% and 13.95%, respectively.

Across the entire bank, the gross NPL (non performing loans) balance rose 6.1% from June to P68.05 billion. Neither blanket pessimism nor an uncomplicated narrative of recovery fits these divergent figures.

An accounting NPL coverage ratio of 89.57%, compared to 113.05% under broader regulatory guidelines, does not by itself prove inadequate reserves. Underlying collateral values, expected recoveries, and precise reserve definitions matter tremendously.

To know if this growth is turning into bad debt, investors need the real numbers behind it: which loan batches are defaulting, which debts are being rewritten, how much is being written off, and how much cash is actually being collected.

Management attributes recent staging recalibrations to Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas findings and notes a P2.7 billion year-to-date expected credit loss impact from macroeconomic assumptions carried over from June.

The underlying regulatory documents and an independent allowance reconciliation are still essential to test those explanations. Forward-looking provisioning and deteriorating borrower repayment capacity frequently coexist; the presence of one does not negate the other.

BPI generated an annualized nine-month return on equity of 13.6%. Reclaiming a sustained market premium requires conviction that long-term returns will exceed the cost of equity that shareholders demand for risk.
Lending growth that consumes capital without earning adequate compensating spreads can enlarge an institution while quietly weakening its investment thesis.
Consider a valuation model assuming an illustrative 14% required shareholder return and 5% perpetual growth funded through retained earnings.

Dividing sustainable Return on Equity (ROE) minus growth by the required return minus growth yields a simplified justified price-to-book ratio: 0.78 times at a 12% ROE, and 1.22 times at a 16% ROE. At BPI’s current multiple of 1.10 times book, this framework implies an expected sustainable ROE of roughly 14.9%.
Any shift in underlying risk assumptions alters that equation, and dated equity numbers cannot replace forward-looking estimates.

Our stress test illustrates the earnings sensitivity. Adding P27 billion in incremental credit provisions — equivalent to roughly 1% of the bank’s rounded loan base — would reduce net income and equity by P20.25 billion after a usable 25% tax shield, or approximately P3.82 per share.

That adjustment would absorb about 41% of nine-month earnings. This exercise represents a disciplined balance-sheet sensitivity test, not a definitive prediction of default or an explicit share-price target.

Margin dynamics also warrant scrutiny. Quarterly net interest margin narrowed from 4.70% to 4.56%. While management expects loan yields to gradually catch up with rising deposit costs, borrowers must have the financial stamina to service higher debt loads.
Preliminary 2027 planning points to credit costs near 100 basis points and loan growth around 10%, though corporate budgets remain unfinished.

Balance sheet buffers offer mixed signals. June’s P13.44 billion net-of-tax fair-value reserve loss on debt securities was already charged against equity; deducting it again would double-count the impact.
However, amortized-cost paper carried a separate P5.53 billion unbooked fair-value shortfall. Updated September marks and interest-rate sensitivity schedules remain essential checks.

An indicative Common Equity Tier 1 ratio of 13.9% and a total capital adequacy ratio of 14.7% temper claims of an immediate capital crisis. Still, the proposed P5 billion SIBOL bond issue will raise debt rather than common equity.

Furthermore, LandBank has clarified that Citicore’s P35.014 billion solar syndication is shared equally with BPI and the Development Bank of the Philippines, implying an exposure of P11.67 billion each before verifying actual funding drawdowns and retained risk.
Meanwhile, BPI’s November 3 clarification stated that no definitive agreement or binding commitment currently exists regarding the reported CIMB opportunity.
Buying expansion abroad or domestically demands rigorous inspection of acquired asset quality, goodwill, and post-merger integration costs, not automatic applause.
Go is scheduled to succeed Jose Teodoro “TG” Limcaoco on April 26, 2027, subject to customary regulatory approvals.
Limcaoco still has five months to solidify the balance sheet his successor will inherit.
For shareholders, true confidence will come from dependable, cash-backed profits after all credit costs are absorbed, not from the fleeting euphoria of a one-day market rally.
BPI must earn back its premium the hard way: by proving the durability of its cash collections.
I welcome your views on these and other issues where decisions made in power shape the country’s economic future. – Rappler.com

(This analysis draws from BPI’s October 21 leadership transition announcement and nine-month financial results; the October 27 investor presentation and earnings briefing transcript; BPI’s June 30 SEC Form 17-Q and historical stock valuations; the November 3 PSE clarification on CIMB; LandBank’s October 26 Citicore syndication release; and November 4 closing records and PSE trading data. Management statements remain attributed disclosures. Valuation multiples and stress-test calculations are the author’s independent analytical illustrations, not bank forecasts or formal price targets.)
